axes.model_access:
A coding harness that plugs into many providers. Official `models` and `providers` pages:

OpenCode uses AI SDK and Models.dev, **supporting 75+ LLM providers, and also supports running local models**. The catalog includes:

- 302.AI
- Amazon Bedrock
- Anthropic
- Azure OpenAI
- DeepSeek
- Google Vertex AI
- Groq
- Hugging Face
- llama.cpp
- LM Studio
- Ollama
- OpenAI
- OpenRouter
- xAI
- Z.AI
- ZenMux and more.

Credentials go through `/connect` into `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json`;

`enabled_providers` / `disabled_providers` act as allow/deny lists,
and custom providers can be defined (`npm` + `baseURL`, OpenAI-compatible included);
there is also the official curated list OpenCode Zen. **Local models can be connected** —

the official docs name llama.cpp, LM Studio, Ollama, Atomic Chat.

Note: connecting via a Claude Pro/Max subscription **is not an Anthropic-officially-supported usage**.
axes.runtime:
A local process running in the terminal. Multi-platform installs are provided (macOS Homebrew / Windows Scoop etc.).
Its lifecycle is bound to the terminal session.
axes.local_files:
Coding capability aimed at real code repositories. `read`/`edit`/`write`/`grep`/`glob`
read and write the workspace directly. `grep`/`glob` use ripgrep underneath, **following `.gitignore` by default**.

**Access is confined by default to the working directory at launch** — paths outside it must be explicitly allowed
via `external_directory` in `permission` (e.g. `~/projects/personal/**`).

`read` is allow by default, but **`.env` / `.env.*` are deny by default** (`.env.example` allow).
The `@` key fuzzy-searches project files; file changes have a `watcher` (with configurable `ignore`).

Symbol-level capability comes from the **LSP tool (experimental)**: it needs `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_LSP_TOOL=true`
plus your own LSP servers, supporting goToDefinition / findReferences / hover and more.

**No description of codebase vectorized indexing was found officially** (tools / config / permissions pages checked).
axes.background:
Terminal form, local process, lifecycle bound to the session.

The official docs also have `opencode serve` (a headless HTTP server).
There is also `opencode web` and a desktop app. **They all run on your own machine.**
They expose a session API to clients, including `prompt_async` for async sending. The execution environment is yours,
not a vendor-hosted cloud.

**No cloud background capability that "keeps running after the client closes / survives shutdown" was found officially**
(server page and docs overview checked).
axes.tools:
**Built-in tools are listed item by item officially**:

- bash
- edit
- write
- read
- grep
- glob
- lsp (experimental)
- patch
- skill
- todowrite
- webfetch
- websearch (Exa, requires the OpenCode provider or `OPENCODE_ENABLE_EXA`)
- question

There is also `task` for dispatching subagents.

Built-in agents include:

- build
- plan
- general
- explore
- scout
- compaction
- title
- summary

**MCP integration verified**:
local `type:"local"` and remote `type:"remote"`, with OAuth
dynamic client registration (RFC 7591) and commands like `opencode mcp auth`;
custom tools and plugins (hooks) are also supported.
axes.context:
**ACP (Agent Client Protocol) load capability is its differentiating design** —
preserving model, effort and mode boundaries across restore and fork.

Session mechanics verified: the `/session` API supports creating,
**forking (branching at a given message)**, revert/unrevert and summarize. The TUI has `/undo`, `/redo`, `/share`.

**The compaction policy is configured officially** — the `compaction` item:

- `auto` (default true, auto-compacts the session when context fills up)
- `prune` (deletes old tool output to save tokens, default false)
- `reserved` (compaction buffer)

There are also three built-in agents: compaction / title / summary.
axes.permissions:
**Permission policy verified**: the `permission` config decides per operation whether it runs automatically,
asks for approval, or is blocked — three tiers `"allow"` / `"ask"` / `"deny"`.

Fine-grained per-tool config is supported, with wildcards and object syntax (for bash:
`git *` allow, `rm *` deny, **the last matching rule wins**).

Configurable permission keys:

- read
- edit (covers edit, write, patch)
- glob
- grep
- bash
- task
- skill
- lsp
- webfetch
- websearch
- external_directory
- doom_loop

**Defaults are permissive**: most are allow,
`doom_loop` and `external_directory` are ask; `read` is allow but
`.env` / `.env.*` are deny by default.

The official config page also says "all operations are allowed by default, no explicit approval needed".

The approval UI offers once / always / reject. It can be overridden per agent.

Since v1.1.1 the legacy `tools` boolean config has been merged into `permission`.

sections.权限设计：执行前询问:
This is the single most notable line in this entry, from the README:

```
Asks permission before running bash commands
```

**Most terminal agents execute commands automatically by default; OpenCode asks.**

This lowers the risk of "the model deleting files / running dangerous commands by mistake",
at the cost of interrupting the flow. The README also mentions **YOLO**,
likely an optional no-ask mode,
**but the exact switch was not verified this pass — recorded as unknown**.
sections.子代理能力:
```
Also included is a general subagent for complex searches and multistep tasks.
```

A built-in **general subagent** for complex searches and multistep tasks.
This lets it handle "investigate first, then act" style tasks that need multiple rounds.

**The subagent's scheduling details and token overhead were not verified this pass.**
sections.ACP：Agent Client Protocol:
This is its architectural highlight:

```
ACP load/restore/fork preserves model, effort and mode boundaries (translated from the dossier's Chinese paraphrase)
```

**"Preserving model and effort across forks" is a detail worth noting** —
many tools lose settings after a fork, forcing you to re-set them every time.
sections.稳定性修复是重要信号:
Referring to AgentClash's verification record of OpenCode v1.18.33 (09-28),
that version contains four fixes:

1. Cloudflare timeout control
2. MCP browser launch-failure feedback
3. **debug credential redaction**
4. Gemini reasoning-parameter correction

**Two of the four relate to permissions/reliability** (credential redaction, MCP launch-failure feedback).
This shows the project's reliability investment goes into permissions and diagnosability —
but it also means **these areas had problems before**.
